blockMcqs.question: What is the one non-negotiable requirement for binary search?
options: The array must hold unique values
The data must be sorted or monotonic
The array length must be a power of two
The values must be integers
blockMcqs.explanation: Order is what lets the middle element reveal which half to discard.

blockMcqs.question: Why does binary search run in O(log n) time?
options: It caches earlier comparisons
Each comparison discards half the candidates
It scans only even indices
Sorted arrays use less memory
blockMcqs.explanation: Halving n candidates k times reaches one when 2^k equals n, so k is log₂ n.

blockMcqs.question: Why use `mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2` instead of `(lo + hi) // 2`?
options: It rounds toward the target
It is faster on modern CPUs
It avoids integer overflow on large indices
It guarantees mid is never lo or hi
blockMcqs.explanation: lo + hi can exceed the integer max and wrap negative; this form never does.

blockMcqs.question: In the half-open lower_bound, why is the keep branch `hi = mid`?
options: To shrink the window by exactly one
Because mid itself may still be the answer
To skip the overflow check
Because hi is exclusive of mid already
blockMcqs.explanation: A[mid] >= target makes mid a candidate, so it stays inside the window.

blockMcqs.question: How do you count occurrences of x using the two templates?
options: lower_bound(x) + upper_bound(x)
upper_bound(x) - lower_bound(x)
upper_bound(x) - 1
len(A) - lower_bound(x)
blockMcqs.explanation: The two boundaries fence the run of x, so their difference is the count.

blockMcqs.question: What makes a problem solvable by binary search on the answer?
options: The input array is already sorted
A monotonic check over a numeric answer range
The answer is always a power of two
The check runs in constant time
blockMcqs.explanation: A FALSE-then-TRUE feasibility test has one flip point to binary-search for.

blockMcqs.question: When is a hash set a better choice than binary search?
options: When you need range and next-bigger queries
When the data is already sorted
When you need only exact membership, never order
When the array is enormous
blockMcqs.explanation: A hash set gives O(1) lookups but no ordering, so it loses on range queries.

blockMcqs.question: What does `git bisect` use as its monotonic predicate?
options: Whether the commit compiles
Whether the bug is present at a commit
The number of files changed
Whether tests run faster
blockMcqs.explanation: Once introduced the bug stays present, so the answer flips once across history.
